articles.title: The Real Cost of CMMC Was Never the Certification
articles.excerpt: DoD paused CMMC Phase 2 in July 2026 and pointed to cost. Federal News Network has now reported what DoD's own request for information (RFI) shows, from DoD's internal summary of the responses. The da…
articles.body: DoD paused CMMC Phase 2 in July 2026 and pointed to cost. Federal News Network has now reported what DoD's own request for information (RFI) shows, from DoD's internal summary of the responses. The data points somewhere specific: the cost is in the NIST SP 800-171 controls your contract already requires, not in the certification. What the RFI data shows Federal News Network reported, in a two-part investigation published Oct 26 and Oct 27, 2026: DoD reviewed 997 responses, 509 (51%) of them from the defense industrial base.- The average CMMC assessment cost cited by respondents was $47,000.

articles.title: Wie finde ich das kostenlose Volltext-PDF einer Studie anhand ihrer DOI?
articles.excerpt: Du hast eine DOI, die Seite des Verlags verlangt einen Login, und du willst nur den Methodenteil lesen. Sehr oft gibt es irgendwo eine legale, kostenlose Kopie: im Repositorium der Universität der Aut…
articles.body: Du hast eine DOI, die Seite des Verlags verlangt einen Login, und du willst nur den Methodenteil lesen. Sehr oft gibt es irgendwo eine legale, kostenlose Kopie: im Repositorium der Universität der Autoren, als Preprint, in PubMed Central. Von Hand heißt das, vier oder fünf Seiten durchzuprobieren. In Code braucht es eine Handvoll öffentlicher APIs, die in sinnvoller Reihenfolge abgefragt werden. Die Reihenfolge unten ist die des Buttons „View“ im Paper-Workspace der osFoundry -Desktop-App. Deren Backend probiert nacheinander jede Quelle, bis eine ein echtes PDF liefert (die Seite zum Workspace für wissenschaftliches Schreiben und Recherchieren zeigt den Bildschirm drumherum).

articles.title: AI helped you ship faster. Can your users keep up?
articles.excerpt: You shipped three features this week. Great. Can someone who signed up on Monday actually use the first one? That is the part I keep coming back to with AI. We spend a lot of time discussing how much…
articles.body: You shipped three features this week. Great. Can someone who signed up on Monday actually use the first one? That is the part I keep coming back to with AI. We spend a lot of time discussing how much faster we can build. Less time discussing how much more work we are giving the person on the other side of the screen. They still have to understand the product. Set something up. Decide whether to trust the result. Explain it to a colleague. Sometimes get permission before they can do anything useful. None of that disappears because the feature took two days to build. I lead product design and I’m building Cueston , a product for in-app guidance. So yes, I have a commercial interest here.

articles.title: 16,000 databases, and the four ways row-level security silently fails

articles.body: In late September 2026, UpGuard researchers reported finding more than 16,000 Supabase databases exposing readable tables containing personal data, passwords, or authentication tokens. They had analysed roughly 300,000 domains for the signature of a Supabase project, then checked whether a users table — or something with another name — answered. The attribution matters more than the number. In the reporting, the researchers point at "poor application security configurations, including missing or ineffective row-level security policies and misuse of public keys" , and add: "The common thread is that these sites are created by AI coding agents and the humans are unaware of the configuration." ( BleepingComputer ) That last sentence is not an accusation about AI.

articles.title: Your First PR Needs Two Test Runs, Not One
articles.excerpt: Your first PR will fail tests you did not break. Most newcomers cannot tell their breakage from pre-existing debt. The fix is boring: record a baseline before you edit, then diff against it. This dril…
articles.body: Your first PR will fail tests you did not break. Most newcomers cannot tell their breakage from pre-existing debt. The fix is boring: record a baseline before you edit, then diff against it. This drill takes about 40 minutes on a repo whose suite runs in under ten. You need git, a clean checkout, and one throwaway machine. You do not need permission to touch CI. Why pass/fail counts mislead a newcomer A red suite tells you nothing about ownership. The count blends your change with old debt, flaky tests, and services that never started. Two runs of the same commit can also disagree. So stop counting failures. Compare sets of normalized failure lines instead. That comparison answers one question: did my edit create this?

articles.title: How we run thirty Claude Code and Codex agents on our own servers (and the tool is now open source)
articles.excerpt: We build Ticksly, a concert ticketing service, and all of our code is written by agents. Up to thirty Claude Code and Codex sessions run at once on our servers. In the last 28 days they opened 2,540 m…
articles.body: We build Ticksly, a concert ticketing service, and all of our code is written by agents. Up to thirty Claude Code and Codex sessions run at once on our servers. In the last 28 days they opened 2,540 merge requests, which comes to about $8 each at API prices. The three of us provide the tasks and the direction. With that many terminal tabs you lose track fast. One agent has been waiting for an answer for a while, another has spent three hours fixing the wrong thing, and the screen doesn't tell you which is which. So since spring we've been building ourselves harnessly, a web UI on top of tmux. The same agents write it, of course: in October they rewrote it from Node to Go in 19 days while still working inside it. Today we're releasing it under Apache-2.0.

articles.excerpt: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is back in communication after the 49-year-old spacecraft briefly fell silent last month, during its interstellar-space mission.
articles.body: Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month. The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix. "This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.

As their Crew Dragon capsule lifted off atop a Falcon 9 rocket that day, Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crewed mission to space. Spaceflight and space science are historically white and male-dominated fields, so this milestone carries incredible significance.
